claims.text: The initial material is a rapidly solidified, non-equilibrium Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy.
The initial alloy has a density below 6 g/cm3.
The initial microstructure contains metastable solid-solution regions and discrete Mg-rich intermetallic compounds.
Controlled annealing can induce phase transformation or decomposition in a high-entropy alloy.
Annealing transforms initially dispersed metastable Mg-rich intermetallic phases into more stable, continuous phases.
The annealed phase distribution becomes more uniform.
The annealing-induced phase rearrangement drives Mg segregation to surfaces or grain boundaries during environmental exposure.
Continuous Mg-rich phases assist formation of a coherent and adherent external oxide scale.
The protective scale is rich in MgO and may contain other protective oxides derived from alloy constituents.
The annealing-induced Mg redistribution catalyzes growth of a continuous protective oxide film.
The continuous protective oxide film reduces aqueous-corrosion kinetics.
The continuous protective oxide film reduces the high-temperature oxidation rate.
Annealed samples will have a more continuous and adherent oxide scale than as-solidified samples.
Annealed samples will have lower corrosion rates in 3.5 wt% NaCl than as-solidified samples.
Annealed samples will show lower oxidation weight gain during high-temperature exposure than as-solidified samples.
The as-solidified baseline's discrete metastable Mg-rich phases produce less continuous or less protective oxide films.
The proposed effect is limited to alloys below 6 g/cm3 and to the tested salt-corrosion and high-temperature oxidation conditions.
